title: BSE Shares Slide as NSE Plans to Allow Trading of Its Own Stock After Listing
excerpt: Bloomberg reports NSE may permit its shares to trade on its own platform, potentially shifting volumes and reshaping the competitive dynamics between Indias two largest exchanges.
body:
• BSE shares fell nearly 2% after Bloomberg reported that NSE may allow its stock to trade on its own platform after listing on rival BSE, potentially shifting trading volumes.
  • NSE has filed for an estimated $3 billion IPO targeting a September listing, subject to SEBI approval and resolution of legacy governance issues.
  • BSE countered by announcing an agreement with MSCI to explore index-linked derivatives in India, aiming to boost liquidity on its platform.
  • NSE's equity options market share fell from 96.9% in FY24 to 87.4% in FY25, with BSE capturing the difference after regulatory changes.

BSE shares reversed early gains and ended nearly 2% lower on August 20 after Bloomberg reported that the National Stock Exchange may allow its own shares to trade on its platform — a move that could reshape the competitive dynamics between India's two dominant stock exchanges.

According to people familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg, the plan would see NSE list its shares on BSE first, then permit trading on its own platform. The strategy could eventually shift volumes and pave the way for NSE stock's inclusion in the exchange's benchmark indexes, including the Nifty 50.

NSE's $3 Billion IPO Push

The report comes as NSE pushes ahead with what would be one of India's largest-ever initial public offerings. The exchange filed for an estimated $3 billion IPO earlier this year, targeting a September listing subject to approval from SEBI.

However, the offering has faced delays. SEBI has yet to issue a no-objection certificate for the listing, as the regulator continues reviewing legacy corporate governance issues tied to the exchange's former management. Analysts now expect the listing to take place in FY27 rather than the current fiscal year.

NSE's unlisted shares, which surged from approximately ₹1,550 in late March to ₹2,450 by July after the exchange eased transfer rules, have since pulled back sharply. The rally had swelled NSE's investor base nearly fourfold to 159,394 by June, with small investors making up 92% of the total.

BSE's Counter-Move

BSE did not stand idle. Before the Bloomberg report pushed its shares lower, the 150-year-old exchange had announced an agreement with index provider MSCI to explore the launch of futures and options contracts in India linked to MSCI indexes — a strategic move aimed at boosting liquidity and trading activity on its platform.

BSE also launched three new Growth Factor Indices through its arm BSE Index Services: the BSE 500 Growth 50 Index, BSE MidCap 150 Growth 30 Index, and BSE LargeCap 100 Growth 30 Index.

"The market share loss has pretty much run its course now, given that everything that had to happen has happened."

— Ashishkumar Chauhan, CEO, NSE

The Market Share Battle

The exchange rivalry has intensified since SEBI's regulatory overhaul in October 2025, which limited exchanges to just one index options contract per week. NSE was forced to shift its popular Bank Nifty options from a weekly to monthly frequency, retaining only the Nifty options contract.

The impact was immediate. NSE's market share in equity options based on premium turnover dropped from 96.9% in FY24 to 87.4% in FY25, with BSE capturing the rest. NSE CEO Ashishkumar Chauhan has argued the share loss has "pretty much run its course," but analysts at HDFC Securities expect further BSE gains.

BSE also recently introduced a new Closing Auction Session, a 20-minute mechanism replacing the final continuous trading window. SEBI Chairman Pandey warned that any attempt to manipulate the session would face "strict and immediate action."

What's Next

BSE stock closed at ₹3,291.10 on August 20, down 1.82% after the NSE report overshadowed its MSCI announcement. Jefferies has downgraded BSE to "underperform," citing risks to proprietary trading volumes.

The outcome of NSE's IPO — and whether its shares ultimately trade on its own platform — will define the competitive landscape for Indian capital markets. For investors, the exchange battle represents a proxy for broader questions about market structure, liquidity concentration, and regulatory balance in one of the world's fastest-growing equity markets.
